analysis.one_liner: Ends federal income tax on Social Security benefits and pays for it with new payroll taxes on earnings above $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2025 with no cosponsors and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, retirees who have income beyond Social Security pay federal income tax on part of their Social Security benefits. This bill would end that tax entirely, starting the year after it is enacted. To make up the money — and to keep the Social Security and Medicare trust funds from losing the revenue that tax now provides — the bill would impose Social Security payroll taxes on wages and self-employment income above $250,000 a year, which are currently exempt above a much lower cap (about $176,100 in 2025). It would also give people who earn above $250,000 a small extra Social Security benefit for those new contributions, and would shield low-income beneficiaries on SSI and Medicaid from any side effects.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40-plus percent of beneficiaries who now owe income tax on part of their Social Security benefits would keep that money — the savings flow mainly to middle- and lower-income retirees, since the tax already exempts most low-income seniors. Current and future high earners would also gain a small new benefit entitlement: earnings above $250,000, newly subject to payroll tax, would count toward a modest additional benefit (2% of excess earnings in the benefit formula). The bill explicitly holds SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries harmless so low-income seniors do not lose anything from the formula changes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees paying income tax on benefits

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 86 of the tax code, ending federal income tax on Social Security benefits for every current and future beneficiary.
Protects low-income seniors on SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP by holding their benefit levels harmless from the formula changes.
Keeps the Social Security and Medicare trust funds whole by directly appropriating Treasury money equal to the revenue lost from ending the benefit tax.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, employers, and the self-employed with incomes above $250,000 a year would pay Social Security payroll taxes on those earnings with no cap, for both the employee (6.2%) and employer (6.2%) shares. In effect, high earners would take on a new tax that today stops at the annual wage cap. General taxpayers ultimately bear the cost of the Treasury appropriation that replaces trust-fund revenue from the repealed benefit tax, since the bill funds it from money in the Treasury without naming a new revenue source.

drawbacks.text: Workers and employers would pay Social Security payroll taxes on wages above $250,000 with no cap, and the self-employed would face the same levy — a large tax increase for high earners, which opponents would call a tax hike on small-business owners and professionals.

The bill holds the trust funds harmless through a general Treasury appropriation, meaning the money previously paid into Social Security from benefit taxation would come from general federal borrowing or other revenues, adding to the deficit unless offset elsewhere.

High earners who pay the new tax would get only a modest extra benefit (2% of excess earnings in the benefit formula), so the payroll-tax increase above $250,000 is partly a transfer, not a fully matched contribution.
The bill adds complexity: a new tax-return filing for workers with multiple employers whose combined wages top $250,000, and new wage-indexing adjustments to the benefit formula.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — ending income tax on Social Security benefits — goes overwhelmingly to lower- and middle-income retirees, since higher-income beneficiaries pay most of that tax today and would still owe income tax on other retirement income. The cost falls on a genuinely concentrated group: workers and employers paying on wages above $250,000. The trust-fund appropriation and the extended benefit formula keep Social Security roughly whole financially, though the bill never explains how the new general-fund appropriation would be funded, which is the strongest good-faith objection: it substitutes one unfunded obligation for another. As a design matter, the $250,000 threshold is fixed in the statute rather than indexed, so over decades it would capture more middle-income earners unless Congress raises it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in September 2025 and referred to the Finance Committee, which has not acted on it, so it has never come up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on September 4, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No other senator has signed on as a cosponsor.
As of the latest action record, the Finance Committee has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners who would have paid new payroll taxes above $250,000, and the employers of highly paid staff, are better off because the bill has gone nowhere.

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: With no cosponsors, no committee action, and no votes, the record shows no measurable support or opposition in either party yet.

industries.note: They would newly pay the 6.2% employee (and employer) Social Security tax on wages above $250,000, which are currently exempt above the annual cap, and self-employed high earners would pay the corresponding self-employment tax.

industries.industry: Current Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries
industries.note: Retirees and disability beneficiaries would no longer owe federal income tax on their Social Security checks; because the tax falls more heavily on middle- and higher-income beneficiaries, the benefit is concentrated among retirees with other income but is real for anyone who files.

They would pay the employer share of the Social Security tax on each worker's wages above $250,000, a new payroll cost on top-of-market salaries; most businesses with lower-wage workforces are unaffected.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced in the Senate with no cosponsors almost never reach the floor, and the Finance Committee has shown no activity on this one. Unless it picks up cosponsors or a committee chairman takes it up, it will most likely die quietly at the end of this Congress, like most single-sponsor tax bills.
